title: Kubernetes & kubectl
description: Running containers in a cluster: the core objects and the kubectl commands you use every day.
resumo: Kubernetes keeps the declared state: you say what you want, controllers make it so.
Always check the kubectl context before changing anything.
First commands when something is wrong: `get`, then `describe` (read the Events), then `logs --previous`.
Manifests in Git + `kubectl apply`; hand fixes drift and are undone by the next apply.
Pods are ephemeral; Deployments recreate them. Never deploy with `latest`.
Services give pods a stable name; the selector must match the pod labels.
ConfigMaps for config, Secrets for credentials (only Base64); env vars are read at start — `rollout restart`.
`rollout undo` stops the damage; revert in Git too.

subsections.subtitle: Cluster Architecture
subsections.description: The control plane, the nodes and the declarative model.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** twenty containers spread over five servers. When one crashes, or a server dies, someone has to notice and start it again somewhere else — at 3 a.m.

**Concept:** Kubernetes runs containers across a cluster of machines. The control plane holds the `kube-apiserver` (the entry point for every operation, kubectl included), `etcd` (the key-value store with the cluster state), the scheduler (decides which node runs each pod) and the controllers (loops that compare the desired state with the actual state and fix differences). On every node, the `kubelet` runs the pods and `kube-proxy` handles Service networking.

**How it works:** you declare what you want — "3 replicas of this image" — and the cluster keeps it that way. If a pod dies, a controller creates another and the scheduler places it on a healthy node. You describe the "what"; the cluster handles the "how".
examples.code:
kubectl (you)
    │  HTTPS
    ▼
┌──────────── Control plane ────────────┐
│ kube-apiserver ── etcd (state)        │
│ scheduler      controllers (loops)    │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
Node 1: kubelet + kube-proxy + runtime -> pods
Node 2: kubelet + kube-proxy + runtime -> pods
examples.interview_question: How does Kubernetes keep the application in the desired state?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Deleting a pod to stop the application. The Deployment still wants its replicas, so a new pod appears seconds later. Change the desired state instead.
examples.code:
kubectl delete pod api-orders-7d9f8
kubectl get pods
# api-orders-5c2kx   1/1   Running   0   4s     <- a new one, already

# RIGHT: change the desired state
kubectl scale deploy/api-orders --replicas=0    # (or set replicas in the manifest)

subsections.subtitle: Configuring kubectl: kubeconfig and Contexts
subsections.formerSubtitle: Configurando o kubectl: kubeconfig e Contextos
subsections.description: Knowing which cluster you are talking to before any command.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you have access to dev, staging and production. One command typed in the wrong terminal deletes something in production.

**Concept:** kubectl reads `~/.kube/config` (or the files in `KUBECONFIG`), which holds clusters, users and contexts. A context combines a cluster, a user and a default namespace.

**How it works:** check the current context before anything that changes resources, give contexts clear names (dev, staging, prod), and set a default namespace so you do not repeat `-n`. Tools like kubectx and kubens make switching faster.
examples.code:
kubectl version                                   # client and server versions
kubectl config get-contexts                       # list contexts (* = current)
kubectl config current-context                    # check BEFORE changing anything
kubectl config use-context staging                # switch cluster
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=orders   # default namespace
kubectl cluster-info                              # control plane address
examples.interview_question: How do you switch between clusters with kubectl without risking changes to production by mistake?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Trusting that the current context is the one you think. In scripts and risky commands, name the context explicitly.
examples.code:
kubectl delete -f k8s/          # you thought it was dev — the current context was prod

# RIGHT
kubectl config current-context
kubectl --context=dev delete -f k8s/

subsections.subtitle: Inspecting Resources: get, describe and events
subsections.formerSubtitle: Inspecionando Recursos: get, describe e events
subsections.description: The first commands when anything goes wrong.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a pod is not working, and all you see is "not ready". You need the reason.

**Concept:** `kubectl get` lists resources in a short form (status, ready replicas, restarts); `-o wide` adds the node and IP, `-o yaml` shows the whole object, and `-w` watches for changes. `kubectl describe` shows readable details, with an Events section at the end: scheduling errors, image download failures, failing probes. `kubectl explain` documents any field.

**How it works:** when in doubt, `describe` and the events come first: they usually say exactly what is wrong.
examples.code:
kubectl get pods                         # STATUS, READY, RESTARTS
kubectl get pods -o wide                 # + node and IP
kubectl get deploy api-orders -o yaml    # the full object (spec + status)
kubectl get pods -w                      # watch changes live

kubectl describe pod api-orders-7d9f8    # details + Events at the end
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy # documentation of a field
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between kubectl get and kubectl describe?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Looking only at the STATUS column and guessing. The reason is in the events.
examples.code:
kubectl get pods
# api-orders-7d9f8   0/1   Pending   0   5m      <- why?

kubectl describe pod api-orders-7d9f8
# Events:
#   Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory.

subsections.subtitle: kubectl apply and the Declarative Model
subsections.formerSubtitle: kubectl apply e o Modelo Declarativo
subsections.description: Versioned manifests as the source of truth.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** someone fixes production with a quick command; nobody knows it happened, and the next deploy brings the old configuration back.

**Concept:** imperative commands (`create`, `scale`, `set image`, `edit`) change the cluster directly. The declarative model keeps manifests (YAML files) in Git and applies them with `kubectl apply -f`: reproducible, reviewable in a pull request, and the basis for GitOps. `kubectl diff` shows what would change before applying.

**How it works:** imperative commands are still useful for experiments and for generating a first manifest with `--dry-run=client -o yaml`.
examples.code:
kubectl diff -f k8s/          # what would change in the cluster
kubectl apply -f k8s/         # apply every manifest in the folder
kubectl delete -f k8s/        # remove what they created

# Imperative: handy to generate a starting manifest
kubectl create deployment api --image=ghcr.io/shop/api:1.0 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deployment.yaml
examples.interview_question: Why prefer kubectl apply with versioned files over imperative commands?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Fixing the cluster by hand and leaving Git as it was. The cluster and the manifests drift apart, and the next apply silently undoes the fix.
examples.code:
kubectl edit deploy/api-orders       # changed the image to 1.5.0 by hand
kubectl apply -f k8s/                # next deploy from Git: back to 1.4.0

# RIGHT: change the manifest in Git, review it, apply (or let GitOps sync it)

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** Kubernetes does not run containers directly. You need to know what it runs, and why pods come and go.

**Concept:** a pod groups one or more containers that share the network (one IP, talking over localhost) and volumes. Pods are ephemeral: if the node fails or the pod is removed, it does not come back by itself, and a new pod gets a new IP. That is why applications run under controllers — Deployment, StatefulSet, Job — that recreate pods automatically.

**How it works:** normally one application container per pod. `kubectl run` is useful for quick tests and debugging inside the cluster.
examples.code:
# A temporary pod to test connectivity inside the cluster
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sh
# inside the pod:
wget -qO- http://api-orders.orders.svc.cluster.local:8080/actuator/health

kubectl get pods -o wide        # pod IP and the node it runs on
examples.interview_question: Why are pods usually not created directly?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Running an application as a bare pod. When the node is drained or fails, the pod is gone and nothing recreates it. Use a Deployment.
examples.code:
# WRONG: a bare pod
kubectl run api --image=ghcr.io/shop/api:1.4.0

# RIGHT: a Deployment recreates pods and keeps the replica count
kubectl create deployment api --image=ghcr.io/shop/api:1.4.0 --replicas=2

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** one cluster runs dozens of applications from several teams. You need to separate them and to act on "all the pods of this app" at once.

**Concept:** namespaces separate resources logically — by team, environment or application — and allow quotas and permissions per namespace. Labels are key-value pairs on any object. Selectors use labels to connect resources: a Service finds its pods by label, and a Deployment its ReplicaSets.

**How it works:** in kubectl, `-n` picks the namespace, `-A` means all namespaces, and `-l` filters by label, which makes commands over a group of resources simple.
examples.code:
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl create namespace orders
kubectl get pods -n orders
kubectl get pods -A                          # all namespaces

kubectl get pods -l app=api-orders           # filter by label
kubectl get pods -l 'env in (staging,prod)'
kubectl label pod api-orders-7d9f8 version=1.4.0
kubectl get pods --show-labels
examples.interview_question: What are labels and selectors for in Kubernetes?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Forgetting the namespace. kubectl looks in the context's default namespace (often `default`) and says nothing exists. Pass `-n`, or set the default namespace once.
examples.code:
kubectl get pods
# No resources found in default namespace.     <- the app is in "orders"

# RIGHT
kubectl get pods -n orders
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=orders

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you need three copies of the API running at all times, and a way to update them without downtime.

**Concept:** a Deployment declares the image, the number of replicas and the update strategy. It creates a ReplicaSet, which makes sure that many pods with that template are always running. Each change to the template (a new image, a new variable) creates a new ReplicaSet, and pods move to it gradually (rolling update); old ReplicaSets are kept so you can roll back.

**How it works:** change the replica count in the manifest. `kubectl scale` is for quick adjustments and is undone by the next apply. A HorizontalPodAutoscaler adjusts the count by load — it needs `resources.requests.cpu` on the container.
examples.code:
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-orders
  labels: { app: api-orders }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api-orders }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api-orders }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/shop/api-orders:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080

# Commands
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -l app=api-orders
kubectl scale deploy/api-orders --replicas=5    # quick, undone by the next apply
kubectl autoscale deploy/api-orders --min=3 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70
examples.interview_question: What is the relationship between a Deployment, a ReplicaSet and a Pod?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Deploying with the `latest` tag. You push a new "latest" and apply, and nothing happens: the template did not change, so there is no rollout — and different pods may run different builds. Use a new tag for each version.
examples.code:
# WRONG
image: ghcr.io/shop/api-orders:latest
# push a new "latest" + kubectl apply -> no rollout: the template is identical

# RIGHT
image: ghcr.io/shop/api-orders:1.5.0

subsections.subtitle: Services: Stable Address and Load Balancing

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** pods change IP every time they are recreated. How does another service find them?

**Concept:** a Service gives a group of pods a stable DNS name and virtual IP, and spreads traffic across the pods that match its label selector. `ClusterIP` (the default) is reachable only inside the cluster — ideal between microservices; `NodePort` opens a port on every node; `LoadBalancer` asks the cloud provider for a load balancer. Inside the cluster the name is `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`.

**How it works:** clients call the Service name, never a pod IP. `port` is what clients use; `targetPort` is the container's port.
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-orders
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector: { app: api-orders }   # sends traffic to pods with this label
  ports:
    - port: 80                    # Service port
      targetPort: 8080            # container port

kubectl get svc
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api-orders   # the pods behind it
examples.interview_question: Why should an application not call a pod's IP directly?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A selector that does not match the pod labels. The Service exists but has no endpoints, and every request fails. Compare the selector with `--show-labels`.
examples.code:
# Service selector:  app: api-orders
# Pod labels:        app: orders-api           <- no match

kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api-orders
# ENDPOINTS: <unset>                           -> requests fail

kubectl get pods --show-labels                 # compare and fix one of them

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the same image must run in every environment; only the configuration changes. Baking URLs and passwords into the image means one image per environment.

**Concept:** ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive values and Secrets hold credentials. Both can become environment variables (Spring Boot maps `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` to `spring.datasource.url`) or mounted files. Secrets are only Base64-encoded, not encrypted: control access with RBAC, and never commit them in plain text.

**How it works:** reference them from the container with `envFrom`, or one key at a time with `valueFrom`.
examples.code:
kubectl create configmap api-config \
  --from-literal=SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  --from-literal=SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop

kubectl create secret generic api-secrets \
  --from-literal=SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD='change-me'

# In the Deployment's container:
#   envFrom:
#     - configMapRef: { name: api-config }
#     - secretRef:    { name: api-secrets }

kubectl get configmap api-config -o yaml
examples.interview_question: How do you pass configuration and credentials to a Spring Boot application in Kubernetes?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Changing a ConfigMap and expecting the running pods to see it. Environment variables are read only when the container starts. Restart the rollout.
examples.code:
kubectl edit configmap api-config         # change SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
# the running pods still have the old value

# RIGHT: new pods read the new values
kubectl rollout restart deploy/api-orders

subsections.subtitle: Logs, exec and port-forward
subsections.description: Debugging the application inside the cluster.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the application misbehaves inside the cluster, where you cannot just open a terminal or a browser.

**Concept:** `kubectl logs` shows the current container's output; after a crash, `--previous` shows the run that died, which usually contains the error. `-f` follows live and `-l` gathers several pods. `kubectl exec` runs commands inside a container (distroless images have no shell — use `kubectl debug`). `kubectl port-forward` opens a private tunnel from your machine to a pod or Service.

**How it works:** use port-forward to reach Actuator or a database for a moment, without exposing them.
examples.code:
kubectl logs api-orders-7d9f8                 # current logs
kubectl logs api-orders-7d9f8 --previous      # logs from before the last restart
kubectl logs -f deploy/api-orders             # follow one pod of the Deployment
kubectl logs -l app=api-orders --tail=50      # last lines of every pod

kubectl exec -it api-orders-7d9f8 -- sh       # shell in the container
kubectl exec api-orders-7d9f8 -- env          # environment variables

kubectl port-forward svc/api-orders 8080:80   # http://localhost:8080
kubectl cp api-orders-7d9f8:/tmp/heap.hprof ./heap.hprof
examples.interview_question: How do you see the logs of a container that restarted?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Exposing a database publicly "just to check something". It is easy to forget, and it is open to the internet in the meantime. Use port-forward: a private tunnel that closes with Ctrl+C.
examples.code:
# WRONG
kubectl expose deploy/postgres --type=LoadBalancer --port=5432

# RIGHT
kubectl port-forward svc/postgres 5432:5432

subsections.subtitle: Updates and Rollback with kubectl rollout
subsections.formerSubtitle: Atualizações e Rollback com kubectl rollout

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a new version goes out and errors start. You need to see whether the rollout finished — and to go back quickly.

**Concept:** changing the image starts a rolling update. `kubectl rollout status` follows it to the end and fails if it gets stuck, which is useful in CI. `kubectl rollout undo` goes back to the previous revision, or to a specific one with `--to-revision`. `rollout restart` recreates the pods without changing the image — for example, to pick up a changed Secret.

**How it works:** `rollout history` lists the revisions kept by the Deployment.
examples.code:
kubectl set image deploy/api-orders api=ghcr.io/shop/api-orders:1.5.0
kubectl rollout status deploy/api-orders --timeout=5m
kubectl rollout history deploy/api-orders

kubectl rollout undo deploy/api-orders                  # back to the previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api-orders --to-revision=3
kubectl rollout restart deploy/api-orders               # recreate the pods
examples.interview_question: How do you roll back a bad deployment?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Rolling back in the cluster and leaving Git as it was. Git still says 1.5.0, so the next pipeline run redeploys the broken version. Undo to stop the damage, then revert the change in Git.
examples.code:
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api-orders     # production is back on 1.4.0...
# ...but the manifest in Git still says 1.5.0

# RIGHT
git revert <commit-that-bumped-to-1.5.0>
git push
